g.passage: Saga had been folding dumplings wrong for three weeks before she told me about the offer. A hotel kitchen in Seoul wanted her, with a salary I could not match and a uniform with her name stitched on the pocket. I said nothing for a while and kept skimming the broth, which needs skimming whether or not anyone is leaving. When I was her age, I left a stall like this one and came back after a year, ashamed of how little the city had taught me. I did not tell her that. Some lessons spoil when they are handed over. Instead I showed her once more how to pinch the edge so the seam holds in boiling water, and I watched her hands rather than her face. Outside, the wind off the harbor rattled the plastic awning, and a customer called for a second bowl.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Saga's offer?
options: Open resentment toward Saga for considering a job that would leave the stall short of help
Quiet relief that Saga will soon leave a stall where she has struggled to learn the work

g.passage: When Amelie arrived at the laundromat on Calle Feria each afternoon, her grandfather Ivan was already scolding the dryers in a language she was only half learning. He had kept the place open for thirty-one years, through two floods and a decade in which the neighbors bought machines of their own. His ledger was a schoolchild's notebook, and its columns had been thinning for years; still he wrote the day's few coins in a careful hand, as if neatness might persuade the numbers. Amelie practiced verbs by reading his labels aloud: wash, wait, return. He corrected her accent with more patience than he ever showed the machines. Neither of them mentioned the letter from the landlord, folded under the coin tray where it had rested for a month. Down the street, a bakery lowered its shutter, and the smell of anise drifted in with the heat.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Ivan's efforts to keep the laundromat open?
options: Mocking, treating his careful bookkeeping as proof that he misunderstands basic arithmetic
Admiring, presenting his persistence as certain to restore the business to its old success
Indifferent, recording his habits without hinting that the business faces real difficulty
Tender yet realistic, honoring his diligence while noting signs that the business is failing

g.passage: Film canisters rattled on the shelf when the power died, and I found myself stuck in a projection booth in Lima with a stranger named Sipho, who had come to repair the lens. For two hours we waited for the street to come back on. He told me that in his family a goodbye was never said at the door; you walked the guest to the corner, so the parting happened in open air. I had always considered such rituals a little theatrical. Yet when the lights returned and he packed his tools, I caught myself following him down the narrow stairs, past the ticket window, all the way to the end of the block. I am still not sure whose custom I was honoring. A bus went by with its windows fogged, carrying no one I knew.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Sipho's custom of parting?
options: Former skepticism that has softened into a reluctant, almost unconscious acceptance
Steady contempt for a custom that the narrator regards as needlessly theatrical
Nostalgic longing for a family tradition the narrator practiced as a young child
Polite curiosity that never affects how the narrator actually behaves toward Sipho
g.explanation: 화자는 처음에 그런 의식을 '다소 연극적'이라고 여겼다고 밝힌다. 그러나 불이 들어오자 자신도 모르게 Sipho를 따라 골목 끝까지 걸어가며, 누구의 관습을 따른 것인지 모르겠다고 말한다. 두 부분을 연결하면 회의가 무의식적인 수용으로 바뀐 A가 정답이다. B는 앞부분만 본 오답이고, C는 지문에 없는 어린 시절을, D는 실제 행동 변화를 무시한다.

g.passage: Aunt Themba never wasted water. Each morning in the community garden off Mirpur Road, she filled one dented can and divided it among the chilies, the gourds, and Edith's struggling mint, giving the mint the least. Edith, who cooked for the stall her aunt ran, assumed this was a judgment on her. That afternoon a neighbor mentioned, as if everyone knew, that Themba had once given up a place at a teachers' college so that Edith's mother could finish school instead. Edith said nothing. Later, watering alone, she noticed that her aunt's own plot, the farthest from the tap, had always received the last and smallest share. A rickshaw bell sounded beyond the fence, and pigeons lifted off the tin roof of the tool shed.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how Edith learns that a neighbor knows private details of her family's past
To show Edith beginning to see her aunt's strictness as a pattern of quiet self-denial

g.passage: Who pays a tutor in oranges? Miriam had asked this aloud the first week, when Fiorella refused her envelope of coins and accepted only a sack of fruit from the barge's hold. Since then the tutor had come every Thursday, climbing down the ladder with her books wrapped against the river damp, and Miriam's brother had begun reading the cargo lists to the crew with sudden pride. Miriam kept the coins in a tin, telling herself she would insist next time. But this evening she found her brother's old shoes, the pair that had split at the toe, replaced by a sturdy one, with a note in Fiorella's handwriting tucked inside: outgrown by my nephew. Miriam set the tin back on its shelf, unopened. Along the bank, a crane swung a pallet of cement toward a waiting truck.

g.passage: Moira and I spent most of one winter competing to sell pastries in the lobby of a cinema in Samarkand that showed films only on weekends. Each Friday I arrived early to claim the table beside the poster of a forgotten comedy, and each Friday she was already there, her trays set out in tight rows. I used to count her customers instead of serving my own. In February the projector broke, and for three weeks no one came at all. We sat on opposite benches, then on the same bench, trading samples out of boredom. I learned that she folded her dough twice where I folded mine four times, and that her version was better. When the films returned, I set up wherever there was space. Snow slid from the marquee in long, soft sheets.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the narrator's rivalry with Moira over the best table in the cinema lobby

seed.conflict: over an unspoken agreement to avoid one subject
seed.topicSeed: a flooded cellar in Karachi; twin brothers dividing a house over an unspoken agreement to avoid one subject

g.passage: When the monsoon filled our cellar in Karachi, my twin, Nadeesha, and I had been dividing our late father's house for two months without once mentioning why he had left it to us in equal halves. We split the furniture by alternating choices, the books by shelf, the kitchen by drawer. Every list was polite and complete, and none of it touched the subject. The flood made lists useless. We waded in together, passing up boxes neither of us had labeled, and in one of them were letters he had written to each of us and never sent. We read them sitting on the stairs, our feet still in the water, and for the first time that year we argued, loudly, about him. By evening the pump had begun its slow work, coughing brown water into the lane.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show how an accident broke the careful silence that had shaped the twins' dealings
To recount the method the twins used to divide their father's furniture and books
To describe the damage that a monsoon flood caused to a family home in Karachi
To suggest that arguments between siblings are a healthy part of every family's grief

seed.relationship: a retired judge and a young clerk
seed.conflict: when a rumor reaches the wrong person
seed.topicSeed: a mountain bus stop in Hanoi; a retired judge and a young clerk when a rumor reaches the wrong person

g.passage: Rumors travel faster than buses. Xinyi, who had spent thirty years as a judge before retiring to the hills outside Hanoi, knew this better than most. Waiting at the mountain stop, she watched Nguyen, the young clerk from the district office, climb the road with his jaw set. Someone had carried to the landlord's wife what Nguyen had said about the landlord, and now the whole village was repeating it. Xinyi offered him half her bench. She had learned long ago that a story repeated often enough grows teeth, and that once it bites, no ruling can unsay it. She told him to apologize before evening, plainly and without excuses. Below them, mist filled the valley, and the bus horn sounded around the last bend.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “grows teeth” most nearly suggests that a repeated story

loses its details until it no longer resembles the original remark

seed.relationship: an uncle and a nephew with a debt

g.passage:
By noon the riverbed is a road of cracked plates,
and Clement crosses it the way he pays his debts:
slowly, one stone at a time, never looking back.
Bogdan follows with the letter in his pocket,
the apology he wrote in March and never sent,
its corners softened now to cloth.
He owes his uncle money, and something more,
a sentence he carries like a stone in a shoe,
small enough to hide, too sharp to forget.
On the far bank a goat chews a plastic bag,
and the heat makes the hills tremble.

g.passage: Secateurs clicked down every row of the vineyard that March in Auckland, but between Leilani and me there was only silence. She had taught me piano for six years, and when she invited me to play at her farewell concert, I said no, too quickly, and then could not explain why. For the whole harvest we worked the same slope without a word. Our silence was a vine grown across the path: each day it thickened, and each day it was harder to step over. I told myself she would speak first. She did not, and on the last afternoon I found her bucket left beside mine, half full of the grapes I had missed. I carried both to the truck. Wasps hung drowsy over the crushed fruit on the tarps.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a vine grown across the path” most nearly suggests that the silence between Leilani and the narrator
options: was a natural part of the quiet, focused work of harvesting grapes
protected the narrator from having to explain her refusal to anyone
became a more stubborn obstacle the longer it was left alone

g.passage: We had argued for weeks about the table. I wanted the terrace laid the Galician way for my mother's visit, with octopus on wooden plates and bread torn by hand; Genevieve insisted on the long French lunch her grandmother used to serve, course after careful course. Both of us worked nights at the hospital, and we fought the way tired people fight, in clipped sentences over cold coffee. I kept a list of every dish she rejected. Then, on the morning itself, I watched her mother teaching mine to fold a crêpe, the two of them laughing at the mess, and the list in my pocket seemed suddenly small and a little foolish. We set out both kinds of plates. Below the terrace, the vines dripped from the night's rain.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?

g.passage: Rain beaded on the manuscript pages Jiayi had carried to the stone bridge, and she shielded them with her sleeve while Haoran read. He had translated four of her novels and praised every ending. Tonight he praised the river, the lanterns, the noodle shop behind them, everything except the final chapter. Jiayi laughed and teased him for turning into a poet. Then he handed the pages back without a word about them, and she understood. The ending she had rewritten six times was still wrong, and he had been too kind, for too long, to say so. She stood very still while the traffic hissed over the wet stones. A boy on a scooter honked twice at nobody.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?

From quiet sadness to growing excitement about rewriting the ending
